title: Equilibrium in a Failed Cartel: Set-Valued Reactions and Sources of Market Asymmetry
content: Cartels may partially collapse when one firm abandons a collusive agreement while the remaining firms continue to coordinate their production decisions. Such market structures naturally lead to coupled optimization problems in which firms’ optimal responses need not be unique. Motivated by this observation, we develop a general mathematical framework for failed-cartel models based on set-valued reaction and best-response correspondences. We first establish an abstract equilibrium existence theorem for three interacting optimization problems under continuity, quasi-concavity, and compactness assumptions. The proof combines Berge’s Maximum Theorem with the Kakutani–Fan–Glicksberg fixed-point theorem and does not require uniqueness of the firms’ optimal responses. The classical failed-cartel Cournot model is then obtained as a direct specialization by verifying that its payoff functions satisfy the hypotheses of the abstract result. For the single-valued case, we derive conditions under which the equilibrium is unique. We further investigate the influence of strategic interactions on equilibrium production. Besides the classical effect of heterogeneous production costs, we identify a purely strategic mechanism showing that, even under identical technologies, the ordering of equilibrium quantities is determined by the sign of the follower’s reaction to the leaders’ production decisions. Depending on this reaction, either the coordinated leaders or the deviating follower becomes the dominant producer. The proposed framework extends the classical analysis of partially coordinated oligopolies and provides a unified mathematical approach for studying equilibrium in failed-cartel markets with both single-valued and set-valued reaction mappings.
